content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates catastrophic overfitting from the perspective of different types of data features. The work divides origin data space into small-scale-feature space and large-scale-feature space with PCA and claims that the over-utilization of small-scale features leads to CO in fast adversarial training. Experiments also show that perturbation lies more in small-scale-feature space after CO. Based on this, the authors propose a method to circumvent CO by removing and perturb the small-scale features in the original dataset. Their method outperforms GradAlign and achieve robust accuracy comparable to multi-step adversarial training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. This paper revisits fast adversarial training from the perspective of data feature, pointing out a big difference of fast AT and PGD-AT.
2. This paper proposes a method to craft a dataset where small-scale features are suppressed, which outperforms GradAlign and achieve robust accuracy comparable to PGD AT.

Weakness:
1. Fig.2(b) shows that there is a correlation between CO and the mutation of the curve(\delta(PGD),  \delta(FGSM), Grad) , but the causality between them is not well explained. It is still unclear whether the overuse of small-scale features is just one result of CO or overuse leads to CO.
2. The method seems to be proposed to prevent CO, but I think it cannot explain why it can achieve such a performance. For example, FGSM-RS augments training data with random noise and can mitigate CO, but the robust accuracy on Cifar10 is just about 45%. There should be more explanation or ablation experiments to explore the reason.  
3. The experimental setup is not common in the field and the results appear a bit confusing: (1)the robust accuracy of FGSM-AT usually drops to nearly 0(like 0.9% or 1.2%) on ResNet18, but accuracy after CO in Fig.4(a) seems above 20%; (2)The test clean accuracy of GradAlign in Table.2 is too low, which is more than 80% in other papers. It kind of makes people wonder if the results were selected; (3)Experiments on wider nets such as WideResNet28-10 should be carried. Anyway, I think the author should change settings where the baseline method performs more normally. Maybe the setting in GradAlign is enough since it is reported in the paper as a method to be compared. 
4. Small advice: There are also some papers exploring the influence of data characteristics on AT, for example "Adversarial examples are not bugs, they are features" or "Catastrophic overfitting is a bug but also a feature".  I think the difference and relation should also be discussed.

content.title: Response to Reviewer DP4c
content.comment:
We are very grateful to the reviewer for your valuable suggestions. First, we need to state that we have adjusted our data augmentation protocol based on suggestions from other reviewers. The new scheme is to simultaneously add uniform random noise in all SVD eigenvectors instead of only operating on small-scale feature dimensions. We call this technique Feature Space Data Augmentation (FDA). The reason why the new scheme is effective is that adding noise in all eigenvectors can not only weaken the correlation between small-scale features and data labels, but also increase data in large-scale feature directions. Furthermore, no additional parameters may be required compared to previous schemes.

1.  Relationship between CO and small-scale features

The adversarial samples generated during the adversarial training process are actually continuously adjusting the distribution of the original samples, so that the model can use reasonable features from the data to find a robust classification boundary. The direction of adversarial perturbation determines how the distribution of the original samples is adjusted. Therefore, we have reason to believe that there is a large difference in the direction of the adversarial perturbations generated during FGSM AT and PGD AT training, which leads to different robustness of the final models. On the other hand, in fact, many current studies have shown that the decision boundary is too parallel to the manifold, which can easily lead to the vulnerability of the model. The decision boundary and the manifold are almost parallel, which means that the model relies too much on small-scale features. However, our experiments prove that by constraining small-scale features, the CO problem can be alleviated and the effect of FGSM confrontation training can be improved.

2. The method seems to be proposed to prevent CO, but I think it cannot explain why it can achieve such a performance. For example, FGSM-RS augments training data with random noise and can mitigate CO, but the robust accuracy on Cifar10 is just about 45%. There should be more explanation or ablation experiments to explore the reason.

First we have to admit that there is a problem with our code. During adversarial training and robustness testing, we did not pass data labels, which caused the adversarial attack algorithm to attack based on the predicted labels of the model.

After we confirmed that the code was correct many times, we tested multiple models under the new data augmentation scheme. Our resnet-18 model adversarially trained with FDA+FGSM achieves a robust accuracy of 48% on CIFAR-10, which is indeed higher than the 46% of FGSM+RS. We believe this may be a benefit of FDA data augmentation. Because the infinite norm regions of feature space and pixel space do not completely overlap, samples from these non-overlapping regions are helpful for model training. Adding uniform random noise to all feature vectors after SVD decomposition can not only weaken the correlation between small-scale features and data labels, but also increase samples in the large-scale direction. The improvement of model performance brought about by data augmentation.


3． There are problems with the accuracy of multiple experimental results

Following the reviewer's suggestion, we revisited our code. There is indeed a problem with our code. We forgot to pass data labels when performing robustness testing, which caused our robust accuracy to be high. After retuning the code, the PGD robust accuracy of the FGSM AT model should indeed drop to 0. We corrected all our experimental results. After retraining the GradAlign method, the clean accuracy of the resnet-18 model on CIFAR-10 is 80.06%. After retraining the GradAlign method, the clean accuracy rate of the resnet-18 model on CIFAR-10 is 80.06%, and the robust accuracy rate is 45.23%, which is very close to the accuracy rate of the original paper.

Using our FDA technology combined with FGSM adversarial training, wideresnet-34-10 can achieve 49.43% robust accuracy and 84.26% clean accuracy on cifar10.


4. Small advice: There are also some papers exploring the influence of data characteristics on AT, for example "Adversarial examples are not bugs, they are features" or "Catastrophic overfitting is a bug but also a feature". I think the difference and relation should also be discussed.

According to the suggestions of experts, we have added the following two literature summaries in the Introduction section. Essentially, small-scale features can be considered as non-robust features.

[2] Andrew Ilyas et.al., Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features, NeurIPS 2020

[3] Harshay Shah et.al, The Pitfalls of Simplicity Bias in Neural Networks, NeurIPS 2020.

content.title: Some questions about the new revision.
content.comment:
In the new revision, the authors adjust data augmentation and propose a new method FDA, which achieve good performance. Since it's a major revision, there are many details not explained clearly. I have the following questions:
1. Compared to the old methods, FDA add noise in the Feature Space on **all** coefficients. Although FDA have good performance,  it is not closely related to the interpretation of small-scale features, which makes the article not very logical, especially the effects of noise on large-scale features are not explored and explained.
2. The reason why FDA works is still not clear. 
- What's the relationship of FDA and label noise? Since FDA add noise on the entire Feature Space, the correlation between data labels and **not only small-scale features but all-scale features** is disrupted. As far as I know, pure label noise can also mitigate CO in some settings. 
- Since FDA augments data, does FDA work because of the **large noise** instead of **noise in Feature Space**?  [1] suggests adding large noise in **Image Space** and not clipping after adding single-step adversarial perturbation can avoid CO. So if FDA can constrain $x_i{\prime}$(noised sample) and $x_i{\prime} + \delta_i$ (noised sample with adversarial perturbation)in the $\epsilon$-ball of $x_i$(origin sample), it will be more convincing.
3. The result of AA suggests that FDA may lead to gradient masking. Authors should provide more experiment result to discuss it.
4. in the explanation of "The difference in direction between different perturbations of a single model" in Section 4, the authors just provide a Grad Alignment experiment to explain why $\delta_{FGSM}$ and $\delta_{PGD}$ also fall in small-scale space but the model still lost robustness to PGD. I think there should be more quantitative experiments. For example, $\delta_{FGSM}$ fall in one subspace of small-scale space while  $\delta_{PGD}$ fall in another subspace.

[1]de Jorge, P., Bibi, A., Volpi, R., Sanyal, A., Torr, P., Rogez, G., & Dokania, P. K. (2021). Towards fast and effective single-step adversarial training.

display_title: Response to Reviewer DP4c For Question 1

content.title: Response to Reviewer DP4c For Question 1
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your reply. We failed to explain the relationship between small-scale features and CO, and why FDA is effective. Next, we try our best to explain them with a simple toy example:

1．Suppose a three-dimensional classification problem (x1, x2, x3), where x1 is a large-scale feature, and x2 and x3 are small-scale features. The three-dimensional features of the first class samples are set as follows: x1 of 98% of the samples obeys the Gaussian distribution N(u, a1), and x1 of the remaining 2% of the samples obeys the Gaussian distribution N(-u, a1). The x2 feature obeys the Gaussian distribution N(u2, a2), where u2 is a small positive number, a2 is also small but x2 is guaranteed to be bigger than 0. The x3 feature is equal to 0.
The characteristics of the second class sample are set as follows: x1 of 98% of the samples obeys the Gaussian distribution N(-u, a1), and the x1 of the remaining 2% of the samples obeys the Gaussian distribution N(u, a1). The x2 feature is equal to 0. The x3 feature obeys the Gaussian distribution N(u2, a2), where u2 is a small positive number, and a2 is also small but guarantees that x3 is bigger than 0。

At this time, the model cannot reduce the loss to 0 only by relying on x1 for classification. If only relying on x2 and x3 then the model will have 100% accuracy. Since x2 and x3 are small, if these two features are to be used for classification, the importance of the features of these two dimensions must be very large, which will lead to a phenomenon of over-reliance on small-scale features.
In order to further illustrate that small-scale features will lead to CO, here we ignore x1, assuming that the model is classified by the following formula：f(x) = w2ReLU(x2-0.5*u2) – w3ReLU(x3-0.5*u2), where w2 and w3 are very large.

In this classification model, due to the existence of ReLU, the gradient of the model on the x2 of the first class sample (the x3 of the second class sample) is 0, which can be considered as a kind of gradient masking. Therefore, the FGSM attack will only reduce the x2 features of the first class to generate adversarial examples ( on the x3 features of the second class). However, the PGD algorithm can attack both x2 and x3. This is why we say that the FGSM adversarial samples and PGD adversarial samples of the model after CO are dominated by small-scale features, but their angles are very large. Considering the low-dimensional manifold structure of the data, there are many dimensions of small-scale features, which will lead to a large difference in small-scale features between FGSM and PGD adversarial samples.

Therefore, we believe that the random initialization in the FGSM-RS algorithm and our operation of adding noise on small-scale features are both to avoid the gradient masking problem on small-scale features. We must emphasize that FGSM-RS can still catastrophically overfit if run long enough. But our plan will not. This shows that adding noise to small-scale features may be a better way. The noise in the sample space cannot reflect the distribution of the data, so it cannot deal with small-scale features well. Therefore, if the FGSM-RS runs for too long, the model will still find loopholes in small-scale features.

If we add noise to the x3 of the first class to activate the ReLU(x3-0.5*u2) neuron, then the FGSM algorithm will attack on both x2 and x3. As long as the attack is performed on x2 and x3, the model will know that these two features are unreliable, and instead rely on the large-scale feature x1. Therefore, in order to make the FGSM AT model robust, we first need to choose a reasonable attack starting point, which can tell the model that small-scale features are unreliable, and only in this way can the gradient of the model pay more attention to large-scale features. Adding noise on the large-scale feature dimension is mainly used as a way of data augmentation.

Through experiments, we found that adding or not adding noise to the large-scale feature dimension has no significant impact on the performance of the model, so we choose to avoid adding an additional parameter d. For the Resnet-18 model on CIFAR-10, the experimental results without adding noise to large-scale features are as follows: when d=500, the robust accuracy rate of the model is 48.97%, and the clean accuracy rate is 81.3%. When d=1000, the robust accuracy of the model is 48.67%, and the clean accuracy is 81.8%. When using the FDA strategy, the model achieves a robust accuracy of 49.07% and a clean accuracy of 81.26%. Therefore, the selection of d has little effect on the performance of the model. So in the end we decided to use the FDA strategy. We will add the experimental results to the appendix.

content.title: Response to Reviewer DP4c for Other Questions
content.comment:
2.1 What's the relationship of FDA and label noise? Since FDA add noise on the entire Feature Space, the correlation between data labels and not only small-scale features but all-scale features is disrupted. As far as I know, pure label noise can also mitigate CO in some settings.

As far as we know, the FDA has little to do with label noise. First, large-scale features are the main fluctuation directions of the data, so samples can fluctuate greatly in these dimensions. Second, since the projection of the sample on the large-scale feature is much larger than the size of the adversarial perturbation, adding noise to the large-scale feature will not bring great deformation to the original sample so that the label changes. The projection of samples on small-scale features is very small, so adding noise can easily break their relationship with labels.

2.2 Since FDA augments data, does FDA work because of the large noise instead of noise in Feature Space? [1] suggests adding large noise in Image Space and not clipping after adding single-step adversarial perturbation can avoid CO.

Because time was in a hurry at that time, we only considered FDA as data augmentation and conducted adversarial training on this basis. Now we reproject the noised sample with adversarial perturbation to the range of the original sample's adversarial perturbation, and find that the model is also robust. The relevant experimental results are as follows (FGSM-RS requires a step size of 10/255, and our step size is still 8/255): For the Resnet-18 model on CIFAR-10, FGSM-RS can achieve PGD robust accuracy of 46.8% and clean accuracy of 83.2% in the 41st epoch, but the robust accuracy of the model after the 60th epoch begins to drop significantly until it reaches zero. For our model (projected into the perturbed neighborhood of the original sample), the robust accuracy rate of 45.43 and the clean accuracy rate of 85.4% can be achieved at the 41st epoch, and the robust accuracy rate is still 40.5% until the final convergence. If it is not projected into the perturbed neighborhood of the original sample, the model will have a robust accuracy of 48.33% at the 41st epoch, and still have a robust accuracy of 43.6% after convergence. We will add these results to the appendix of the article. 

3. The result of AA suggests that FDA may lead to gradient masking. Authors should provide more experiment result to discuss it.

For AA attack, we used the standard evaluation algorithm provided by RobustBench, including four attack tests of apgd-ce, apgd-t, fab-t, and square.  Regarding the results of WRN-34-10, we imported the model parameters saved at the 41st epoch (the most robust), and the AA recognition accuracy of the model was 33.3%. However, when we imported the parameters saved before the 41st epoch, AA recognition The best accuracy rate is 41%. We adjusted the learning rate of the model at the 41st epoch. This means that some neurons may no longer activate after adjusting the learning rate. However, this phenomenon was not found on other models. This is a very surprising result.  The difference between the WRN-34-10 model and other models is that the model uses Dropout, so we conducted experiments on the WRN-34-10 model without Dropout. For the WRN-34-10 model without Dropout, FGSM AT+FDA can achieve 51.57% robust accuracy and 85.82% clean accuracy. Meanwhile, the test accuracy of AA attack is 48.10%. Because Dropout will randomly kill some neurons, which will cause some features to fail to receive gradients, thus exacerbating the gradient masking phenomenon.


4. in the explanation of "The difference in direction between different perturbations of a single model" in Section 4, the authors just provide a Grad Alignment experiment to explain why  FGSM adversarial examples and PGD adversarial examples also fall in small-scale space but the model still lost robustness to PGD. I think there should be more quantitative experiments. For example,  FGSM adversarial examples fall in one subspace of small-scale space while  PGD adversarial examples fall in another subspace.

Following the reviewer's suggestion, we compute the angle between these two types of adversarial examples generated by the model in the small-scale feature space as well as their angle in the large-scale feature space. For the Resnet-18 model trained by FGSM AT, the cosine value of the angle between these two disturbances projected in the small-scale feature space (d=300) is 0.0215, and the cosine value of their angle in the large-scale feature space is 0.0521 . Since the adversarial examples of the FGSM AT model are dominated by small-scale features (at least 80%), the two perturbations are almost orthogonal in the small-scale feature space. For the PGD AT model, these two values are 0.3874 and 0.6831, respectively.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper6113 by Reviewer sg7Z

content.title: Response to Reviewer sg7Z
content.comment:
We are very grateful to the reviewers for their valuable suggestions. First, we need to state that we have adjusted our data augmentation scheme based on suggestions from other reviewers. The new scheme is to simultaneously add uniform random noise in all SVD eigenvectors instead of only operating on small-scale feature dimensions. We call this technique Feature Space Data Augmentation (FDA). The reason why the new scheme is effective is that adding noise in all eigenvectors can not only weaken the correlation between small-scale features and data labels, but also increase data in large-scale feature directions. Furthermore, no additional parameters may be required compared to previous schemes.

1. What is the benefit of smaller values of d as it appears larger values consistently perform better? 

In fact, under our original framework,the minimum value of d can be set as the minimum number of eigenvectors that can reconstruct more than 95% of the information of the original sample. For example, when d=300, using the first 300 eigenvectors can reconstruct at least 95% of the information of CIFAR-10. Therefore, d can be greater than or equal to 300, but it should not be too large. Too large d may cause more small-scale features to be retained in the processed data set and cannot guarantee the robustness of the final model. For example, for the Resnet-18 model trained on CIFAR-10, the experimental results under different d after modifying our code are as follows. When d=500, the robust accuracy rate of the model is 47.55%, and the clean accuracy rate is 78.9%. When d=1000, the robust accuracy of the model is 48.05%, and the clean accuracy is 80.68%. When d=2000, the robust accuracy of the model is 48.72%, and the clean accuracy is 82.43%. But when d=2000, the model will appear catastrophic overfitting at the 60th epoch, because many small-scale features are still retained in the data (retained from the 500th dimension to the 2000th dimension). Therefore, different d mainly affects the accuracy of the model on the clean test set.

Of course, the parameter d is no longer considered under the new data enhancement. The performance of our model has good results both on the clean test set and on the robust performance. For example: Resnet-18 trained by FDA+FGSM AT has an attack recognition accuracy rate of 48.33% under the PGD infinite norm (8/255)) on CIFAR-10, and the accuracy on the clean test set is 81.26%.

The experimental results of the WideResNet-34-10 model on CIFAR-10 are as follows: the FDA+FGSM adversarial training model has a robust accuracy rate of 51.57% under the attack of PGD, and the accuracy on the clean test set is 85.82%. For more experimental results, please review the revised article.

2. It would be a stronger paper if you included experiments on the l2 norm ball perturbations as well.

Following the reviewer's suggestion, we test the model on CIFAR-10 with a PGD attack under the L2 norm (epsilon = 0.5, alpha = 2.5*epsilon / 100, iter = 100 ). For the Resnet-18 model, the accuracy rate of the model trained by PGD AT is 62.85%, the accuracy rate of the model trained by FGSM AT+GradAlign is 52.95%, and the accuracy rate of the model trained by FDA+FGSM AT is 62.27%.

For the WRN-34-10 model, the accuracy rate of the model trained by FGSM AT+GradAlign is 55.12%, and the accuracy rate of the model trained by FDA+FGSM AT is 62.52%.

We have performed PGD l2-norm attacks on all models, and we will include these experimental results in our paper.

3. It would be a more fair comparison to compare against early-stopped PGD or a state-of-the-art variant of PGD. The difference in performance would certainly be more drastic.

The robust accuracy under the PGD attack recorded in the revised manuscript is the best robust accuracy before overfitting occurs. We know that TRADE is a better version of PGD AT, which can make the WRN-34-10 model have a robust accuracy rate of 56.61% and a clean accuracy rate of 84.92% under PGD infinite norm attacks. As a single-step AT algorithm, FGSM AT is indeed difficult to surpass the effect of PGD AT. In this article, we want to solve the catastrophic overfitting problem of FGSM AT and improve its effect. More we want to emphasize that small-scale features will affect the robustness of the model. The advantage of FGSM AT over PGD AT lies in its training speed. FDA+FGSM AT only needs 43.02 minutes to train a Resnet-18 model with a Lupine accuracy rate of 48%. However, due to the existence of the matrix factorization algorithm, this will affect the extension of our model to large-scale data sets. We are currently looking for an alternative to avoid using SVD decomposition.

content.title: Response to Reviewer sg7Z's Additional Comments
content.comment:
Many thanks to the reviewers for their suggestions. 
Additional comments:
1. I cannot read the plots in Figures 3-5.

We have made changes to the descriptions of Figures 3-5 as suggested by the reviewers. For example: the description of Figure 3 is modified to: On MNIST, LeNet models are trained by STD, FGSM AT, and PGD AT respectively. (a) The recognition accuracy of the model on FGSM adversarial samples and PGD adversarial samples, respectively. (b) The proportion of small-scale features in the gradients (Grad) and the adversarial perturbation of the model. (c) Cosine values between δPGD and δFGSM of the model.

2. The section titles aren’t necessarily informative about the content

Based on the reviewers' suggestions, we have revised all the titles in Sections 3 to 5. For example: the title of Section 3 is changed to "Understanding the Adversarial Example Problem". The title of Section 3 is changed to  "Revisiting FGSM Adversarial Training: Over-reliance on small-scale features". The title of Section 5 is changed to  "Improving FGSM Adversarial Training : Feature Space Data Augmentation (FDA)". 

3. I don’t believe you define the variable “u” in (5)? 

u in Equation 5 is explained in Section 3.1. u represents the eigenvector after SVD decomposition of the data matrix.

4. As suggested by the reviewers, we bolded the best performance in Tables 1-4.

5. I would add some visualizations in the main text (I see you have some in the appendix).

Due to the limited number of pages, we will continue to work hard to modify and present some visualization results in the text.

6. Does the dataset modification result in any difference when training with PGD?

According to our current experiments, we have not found that modifying the data will improve the robust performance of PGD AT. This shows that PGD AT has well controlled small-scale features during the training process. For example: for the Resnet-18 model on CIFAR-10, the best robust performance of the PGD AT we trained is 51.66%, and the clean test set performance is 80.7%. FDA+PGD AT's Resnet-18 has a robust performance of 51.52% and a clean test set performance of 81.23%. FDA's data augmentation can lead to a slight improvement in the accuracy of the model on the clean test set.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper shows that the catastrophic overfitting in FGSM adversarial training is a result of overfitting small-scale features. To prove it, the authors use SVD decomposition on the dataset and show that the gradient of FGSM AT focuses more on the features with small eigenvalues. To this end, the paper proposes to a simple but effective method that randomizes the small-scale feature of the dataset. The method solves the catastrophic overfitting in MNIST, CIFAR10 and ImageNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1. The findings of relationship between catastrophic overfitting and small-scale is interesting and insightful. I can motivate the community to have deeper understanding of the catastrophic overfitting and develop new effective method to counter catastrophic overfitting.

2. The proposed method to solve catastrophic overfitting, while simple, is effective. The catstrophic overfitting does not happen with the proposed solution.

Weakness

1. The experiments are not comprehensive. The paper does not evaluate the robustness with AutoAttack [1], which makes it dubious whether the improvement is the result of gradient masking. And it would be better to include WideResNet-34-10 in the experiments as larger model is easier to suffer from catastrophic overfitting.

2. Despite the relationship of catastrophic overfitting and small-scale feature has not been studies, the relationship between adversarial examples and small-scale feature has been studied in [2]. The paper complete ignores the contribution of previous papers.

3. The clean accuracy of the proposed method is relative low compared with FGSM AT.

4. Lack of ablation study in the choice of $d$. As $d$ is a very important hyperparameter of the method, it would be interesting to see its influence on the final robust accuracy.

5. Training time should be reported as this is a fast adversarial training paper. And I wonder whether the SVD decomposition consumes a lot of time for large scale dataset like ImageNet.

Minors

It seems that the small-scale and large-scale features have some relationship with the easy and hard features in [3]. I would also be interesting to study the training dynamics and fast adversarial training as in [3].

content.title: Response to Reviewer qC9s
content.comment:
We are very grateful to the reviewers for their valuable suggestions. First, we need to state that we have adjusted our data augmentation protocol based on suggestions from other reviewers. The new scheme is to simultaneously add uniform random noise in all SVD eigenvectors instead of only operating on small-scale feature dimensions. We call this technique Feature Space Data Augmentation (FDA). The reason why the new scheme is effective is that adding noise in all eigenvectors can not only weaken the correlation between small-scale features and data labels, but also increase data in large-scale feature directions. Furthermore, no additional parameters may be required compared to previous schemes.


1. The paper does not evaluate the robustness with AutoAttack [1]. And it would be better to include WideResNet-34-10 in the experiments.

Following the reviewer's suggestion, we added an AutoAttack attack test to our Experiments section. Some results are as follows: Resnet-18 trained by FDA+FGSM AT has an attack recognition accuracy rate of 48.33% under the PGD infinite norm (8/255)) on CIFAR-10, and an accuracy rate of 45.1% under AutoAttack attack. 

The experimental results of the WideResNet-34-10 model on CIFAR-10 are as follows: the FDA+FGSM adversarial training model has a robust accuracy rate of 49.43% under the attack of PGD. It has a robust accuracy rate of 33.3% under AutoAttack attack.


2. Despite the relationship of catastrophic overfitting and small-scale feature has not been studies, the relationship between adversarial examples and small-scale feature has been studied in [2]. The paper complete ignores the contribution of previous papers.

According to the reviewer's suggestion, we have added a summary of literature [2] and [3] in the Introduction section.

3．The clean accuracy of the proposed method is relative low compared with FGSM AT.

Under the new data augmentation scheme, the resnet-18 model trained by our method has an accuracy of 81.26% on the clean test set. The FDA+FGSM adversarially trained Wideresnet-34-10 has a clean accuracy of 84.26%. We are very much looking forward to reviewers reviewing the revised manuscript to see more detailed experimental results

4、Lack of ablation study in the choice of d . As d is a very important hyperparameter of the method, it would be interesting to see its influence on the final robust accuracy.

In our new framework, the parameter d is no longer needed. In fact, in our original version of the scheme, d has little effect on the model. This is why we tune our scheme to add uniform random noise in all dimensions. For example, training resnet-18 on CIFAR-10, when d=500, the robust accuracy rate is 49.30, and when d=1000, the robust accuracy rate is  49.89.  By checking the code, we found that the robust accuracy rate of the first version of the scheme is problematic, so the robust accuracy rate is high.

5. Training time should be reported as this is a fast adversarial training paper. And I wonder whether the SVD decomposition consumes a lot of time for large scale dataset like ImageNet.

Under the new scheme, it only takes about 40 minutes to train a resnet-18 model with 48% PGD robust accuracy. Of course, this is not an accurate time, because we corrected the program, ran all the experiments again, and sometimes ran multiple programs on one GPU at the same time. Theoretically speaking, compared with FGSM adversarial training, our algorithm only increases the part of SVD decomposition. Matrix factorization is a rather time-consuming algorithm, which is proportional to the number of elements in the matrix. Therefore our scheme is not suitable for validation on larger datasets. Currently, we are also looking for alternatives to solve the problem of the model's over-reliance on small-scale features.

content.title: Response to Reviewer qC9s  for New Questions
content.comment:
We are happy to receive your responses and comments. Regarding your questions, we will answer them one by one.

1. I do not understand why the authors change their previous methods to FDA. I think the motivations of the two methods are similar. Could the authors provide some comparisons of the two methods to show the difference?

In general, we design two versions of data augmentation, v1 and v2. v1 is the previous version, which first removes small-scale features in the sample, and then adds small-scale feature noise. The v2 version directly adds uniform random noise on all small-scale feature dimensions. The experimental results of the two versions on Resnet-18 (CIFAR-10) are as follows. The pgd robust accuracy and clean accuracy under different d values ​​of the v1 version are: d=500, 47.55% and 78.9%. d=1000, 48.05% and 80.68%. d=2000, 48.72% and 82.43%. Since v1 deletes the small-scale features of the original sample, the larger d is, the more original features are retained in the sample, and the clean accuracy of the model is greater. v2: No matter how d is selected (500, 1000, 2000), the robust accuracy of the model is about 48.5% and the clean accuracy is about 81.5%. Since the v2 version does not remove the small-scale features of the original sample, the model has higher accuracy on the clean test set. And d has little effect on the model performance, so we decided to add noise in all  SVD eigenvectors  dimensions, namely FDA. The v2 version itself does not delete small-scale features, so why can it improve the effect of FGSM AT? FGSM AT is able to resist small-scale features in the early stage of training, but it loses this ability in the later stage of training. Therefore, we believe that as long as the relationship between small-scale features and labels is slightly weakened, it can increase the difficulty of mining small-scale features for FGSM AT. We will add these experimental results to the appendix.

2. The experiments of WideResNet with AutoAttack proves that the robust accuracy of the proposed method cannot generalize to large networks. On WideResNet under AutoAttack, the robust accuracy should be more than 42% achieved by previous papers.

For AA attack, we used the standard evaluation algorithm provided by RobustBench, including four attack tests of apgd-ce, apgd-t, fab-t, and square.  Regarding the results of WRN-34-10, we imported the model parameters saved at the 41st epoch (the most robust), and the AA recognition accuracy of the model was 33.3%. However, when we imported the parameters saved before the 41st epoch, AA recognition The best accuracy rate is 41%. We adjusted the learning rate of the model at the 41st epoch. This means that some neurons may no longer activate after adjusting the learning rate. However, this phenomenon was not found on other models. This is a very surprising result.  The difference between the WRN-34-10 model and other models is that the model uses Dropout, so we conducted experiments on the WRN-34-10 model without Dropout.  For the WRN-34-10 model without Dropout, FGSM AT+FDA can achieve  51.57% robust accuracy and 85.82% clean accuracy. Meanwhile, the test accuracy of AA attack is 48.10%. Because Dropout will randomly kill some neurons, which will cause some features to fail to receive gradients, thus exacerbating the gradient masking phenomenon.

3. Presenting a single number of 40 minutes does not provide useful information to evaluate the efficiency of method. I think the authors had better list the time separately for SVD and training networks.

According to the reviewer's suggestion, we trained the Resent-18 model with different training methods on a single TITAN Xp GPU, and recorded the time consumed by the training. The consumption time for SVD decomposition of Cifar-10 is 38.4538s, and it takes 151.1865s for eigenvalue decomposition of a random 10000*10000 matrix. For the Resnet-18 model, the average training time for one epoch (including training and standard testing and PGD attack testing) is 94.5424s. The average time for FDA+FGSM to train an epoch is 116.2963s. For standard FGSM adversarial training, the average training time for one epoch is 115.2745s. For FGSM AT+GradAlign it takes 158.2522s. For standard PGD-10 adversarial training, the average training time for one epoch is 314.6475s. Therefore, it will take 77.18 minutes for FDA+FGSM AT to train the Resent-18 model (training + testing) to achieve a robust accuracy rate of 48%, and it will take 43.02 minutes if the testing time is not included. We will add this part of the results to our final version of the paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer HGUk
content.comment:
We greatly appreciate the reviewer's detailed comments, and we will give the following answers to your comments and questions:

2. If you do not remove the small-scale features and add the random noise directly, will the FGSM-AT work also?

Our original idea was to directly inject random noise in all small-scale feature dimensions. However, it was found that the standard training (STD) model also relies too much on small-scale features, even exceeding 80%. But we did not try to conduct such experiments on FGSM adversarial training. We analyze because E(x+a)=x where a~Uniform(-epsilon, epsilon)), so directly adding noise cannot eliminate the relationship between small-scale features and labels. So we use the strategy of removing small-scale features and adding random noise to these dimensions. 

According to your suggestion, we try to add noise directly without removing small-scale features on FGSM confrontation training. Experiments found that the trained FGSM AT model still has the same robust effect as the strategy of first removing small-scale features and then adding noise.According to our analysis, because adversarial training itself can resist the model's excessive mining of small-scale features, but FGSM AT will lose this ability in the middle and late stages of training. Therefore, the slightly weakened correlation between small-scale features and labels can provide a good motivation for FGSM AT to continue to suppress the use of small-scale features by the model. 

The experimental results of directly adding noise are as follows: FGSM AT training on the Resnet-18 model on CIFAR-10. When d=500, the robust accuracy rate of the model is 48.97%, and the clean accuracy rate is 81.3%. When d=1000, the robust accuracy of the model is 48.67%, and the clean accuracy is 81.8%. When d=2000, the robust accuracy of the model is 48.55%, and the clean accuracy is 81.62%. Therefore, the selection of d has little effect on the performance of the model.
 
In view of the above experimental results, we readjust our scheme and choose to add uniform random noise to the data samples on all the eigenvector dimensions obtained by SVD decomposition. We refer to this strategy as feature space data augmentation (FDA). The reason why we do this is, on the one hand, because d does not have a great impact on the robustness of the model, and secondly, adding noise to the large-scale feature dimension can be used as data augmentation. Based on this, we re-debugged all our experiments and marked the experimental results in red in the revised article

Some experimental results of FDA+FGSM AT under the new scheme are as follows: The robustness under the PGD infinite norm (8/255) attack of Resnet-18 on CIFAR-10 is 48.91% VS 50.92% of PGD-10 adversarial training. A robust accuracy of 51.57% can be achieved on WideResnet-34-10. Moreover, on our machine, FGSM adversarial training + FDA technique can achieve 48% in 43.02 minutes on Resnet-18. 

1. How about the performance of your method on some larger models or larger datasets, such as wideresnet-34-10, ImageNet?

Following the reviewers' comments, we conduct experiments on WRN-34-10 on CIFAR10. Using our FDA strategy and FGSM AT, the robustness of the model under PGD infinite norm (8/255) attack is 51.57%, and the accuracy on the clean test set is 85.82%.

We must admit that it is very difficult for our method to train on large-scale data sets, because the complexity of Matrix Factorization is proportional to the number of elements in the matrix, which will consume a lot of computing resources and computing time. We want to emphasize that that the model tends to use small-scale features for decision-making, which will affect the robustness of the model. We are also currently looking for alternatives to avoid the direct explicit use of SVD decomposition.

3. In your Figure6, do training and inference both use the larger ϵ?

First of all, I am very sorry that we did not clearly describe the experimental settings in Figure 6, which brought ambiguity to the reviewers. Figure 6 shows the robustness results of the models (adversarial training with a perturbation size of 8/255) for PGD attacks with different perturbation sizes. 

4. The Figure 6 is not that clear and it's difficult to distinguish the various lines.

The number of curves in Figure 6 has been reduced since we have modified the original scheme and the new scheme no longer requires the d parameter. We look forward to your revisiting the revised figure. This figure mainly shows that the model after FDA+FGSM adversarial training (perturbation size during training is 8/255) and the model of PGD adversarial training (perturbation size during training is 8/255)  have comparable robust performance under different adversarial perturbations.

content.title: Response to Reviewer HGUk
content.comment:
First of all, thank you very much for the reviewer's reply. 

We must emphasize that FGSM AT-RS besides using random restart, they also use 1.25*eps as the step size. Second, both FGSM AT-RS and FGSM AT + GradAlign use cyclic learning rates, while we use piecewise linear learning rate settings. For the Resnet-18 model on CIFAR-10 (using the piecewise linear learning rate setting), FGSM-RS can achieve PGD robust accuracy of 46.8% and clean accuracy of 83.2% in the 42st epoch, but the robust accuracy of the model after the 60th epoch begins to drop significantly until it reaches zero. While our scheme still has a robust performance of 43.6% at the end of training. This shows that the random initialization in the pixel space can only suppress the model's exploration of small-scale features to a certain extent, but as the model training time increases, the model will still find loopholes in small-scale features. The reason why FGSM AT-RS uses a large step size is to generate stronger adversarial samples that reach the attack boundary of the original sample, while our scheme does not need a large step size because we just use the noisy sample as a new starting point. Of course, our model is still effective when the step size is 16/255 (the perturbation size is 8/255). FGSM AT+FDA achieves the best robustness of 49.08% and clean test set accuracy of 81.8% on the Resnet-18 model at the 41st epoch. At the end of training The robustness is 43%. However, FGSM-RS suffers from catastrophic overfitting when the step size is 16/255. It must be admitted that FDA+FGSM AT is not suitable for model training under large adversarial perturbation sizes. When the adversarial perturbation size is 16/255, the robust accuracy rate of the Resnet-18 model using the early stopping technique is 25.66%, which is lower than the 28.88% in [2]. The FGSM AT + GradAlign in [2] only ran for 30 epochs. Our experiments found that if the training time of FGSM AT + GradAlign is too long, catastrophic overfitting will also occur, so early stopping must be used. However, they say that there is no need to use early stopping.

Our initial solution (remove small-scale features first and then add noise in small-scale feature dimensions) and the current method FDA can prevent catastrophic overfitting of FGSM AT and improve the robustness of the model. We must emphasize that FDA is not the same as random noise in pixel space. The random noise in the pixel space cannot perceive the small-scale features of the data. The standard FGSM AT can suppress the use of small-scale features by the model in the early stage of training, but it loses this ability in the later stage of training. Therefore, random restart is effective because this randomness increases the difficulty for the model to learn small-scale features and thus can alleviate the catastrophic overfitting problem of the model. But FGSM AT still suffers from catastrophic overfitting if the training time is long enough. FDA is a better strategy than random restart. Although FDA does not completely remove the small-scale features in the sample, adding noise to the small-scale feature dimension can well limit the model's utilization of small-scale features.

The robust accuracy rate of the PGD-10 AT model provided in this paper is 50.92%, which is similar to the accuracy rate in [1] and [2]. What is used in [3] is not a standard adversarial training algorithm. We're not looking at what training techniques help improve the effectiveness of resistance training. To avoid ambiguity, we will use "FDA technology can improve the model robustness of FGSM AT" instead of comparable robustness to PGD AT. However, the robust accuracy rate (45.23%) of the model trained by FGSM AT + GradAlign in this paper is lower than 47.58% in [2].  After many attempts, we readjusted the learning rate (the maximum learning rate was changed from 0.1 to 0.01) , and found that the effect of FGSM+GradAlign could be improved.  After adjustment, the Resnet-18 model has a robust accuracy of 47.17% and a clean accuracy of 80.93%.  We will retrain all models trained with FGSM + GradAlign and modify the experimental results.

[1] Wong E, Rice L, Kolter J Z. Fast is better than free: Revisiting adversarial training[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2001.03994, 2020.
[2] Andriushchenko M, Flammarion N. Understanding and improving fast adversarial training[J]. Advances in Neural Information 
     Processing Systems, 2020, 33: 16048-16059.
[3] Pang T, Yang X, Dong Y, et al. Bag of tricks for adversarial training[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.00467, 2020.
